questions.prompt: How does using a vulnerable driver (BYOVD) to blind Defender differ from the PowerShell Set-MpPreference/Add-MpPreference tampering cluster?
options: BYOVD operates at the kernel level, below where user-mode Tamper Protection can see it, while the PowerShell cmdlets operate at the software/user-mode layer
BYOVD only works on Windows Server, never workstations
Set-MpPreference requires kernel-level driver access to function
questions.explanation: BYOVD's second use case (beyond local privilege escalation) is terminating or blinding Defender's kernel-mode components directly -- a fundamentally different threat model than user-mode PowerShell cmdlet tampering, which Tamper Protection can resist.

questions.prompt: Why is a gap in Defender's own event log with no corresponding 5001 (real-time protection disabled) event considered a stronger signal than a 5001 event itself?
options: It isn't -- a 5001 event is always the stronger signal
It suggests the tampering happened below the layer that would normally log its own disabling, such as a kernel-level driver attack
Gaps in event logs are always caused by disk space issues
5001 events are logged more reliably than gaps
questions.explanation: A 5001 event means Defender itself logged being disabled through a normal channel. A silent gap with no such event suggests something bypassed the layer that would normally generate that log entry -- a more advanced and concerning technique.

questions.prompt: Why does registry-based disabling (DisableRealtimeMonitoring/DisableAntiSpyware keys) leave a different evidence trail than the PowerShell cmdlet route?
options: Registry changes are never logged anywhere
It leaves a registry key write visible in the hive itself and via registry-event logging, rather than a command line or script block an analyst focused on PowerShell logging might be watching for
Registry-based disabling is impossible on modern Windows
questions.explanation: An environment monitoring PowerShell activity closely but not registry writes has a blind spot -- the registry route bypasses PowerShell-specific logging entirely, similar to how Windows Script Host bypasses it in Level 3.

questions.prompt: Why does a tampering attempt against a Tamper-Protected host still deserve full investigation even when the control successfully held?
options: Failed attempts are never worth investigating
The intent to disable or evade Defender was still present, even though the control prevented the change from taking effect
Tamper Protection failures are always false positives
Only successful bypasses generate any logs at all
questions.explanation: A failed tampering attempt still demonstrates clear malicious intent on the host. Confirming the control held is important, but the attempt itself is a red flag independent of whether it succeeded.
